Hate
HAYT
v.
Old English hatian, “to hate, treat as an enemy.” Renders the Hebrew sānē’, “to hate,” and the Greek miseō, “to hate,” used both negatively (the hatred of evil and the hatred Scripture forbids of one’s brother) and positively (the holy hatred of sin and the comparative hatred that prefers Christ above family and self).

📖 Biblical Definition

Hate, in Scripture, has two opposite biblical uses and one biblical use that has long puzzled modern readers. The forbidden hate is the personal malice toward one’s brother that 1 John condemns as walking in darkness: he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because that darkness hath blinded his eyes; and again, whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him. This hate is the inward will-of-injury, the long-nursed bitterness, the settled enmity against another image-bearer; it is forbidden in every form, and its presence in the heart of one who claims to know God is a credible challenge to the claim. The commanded hate is the holy hatred of sin and the works of darkness, set by Scripture as the necessary correlate of the love of righteousness: ye that love the LORD, hate evil; I hate every false way; thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity (Ps 45:7, applied to Christ in Heb 1:9); the saint is to abhor that which is evil (Rom 12:9). Without holy hatred of sin, the love of righteousness atrophies into sentiment; with it, the love of righteousness has the moral seriousness Scripture assumes. The comparative hate is the one that has puzzled modern readers: if any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. The Hebrew idiom of comparative loving and hating (used in Gen 29:30-31 of Jacob loving Rachel and hating Leah—not personal malice, but preferring less) is here applied to the absolute priority of Christ: the disciple loves Christ so supremely that every other love—legitimate, deep, lifelong loves of family and self—is by comparison a hating. The same point is made plainly in Matthew 10:37: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. The verb hate therefore is freighted: forbidden in its personal-malice register, commanded in its holy-hatred-of-sin register, and applied comparatively in the demand for the supreme allegiance Christ requires of His disciples.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HATE as to dislike greatly; to have a great aversion to; opposed to love; in a more moderate sense, to dislike, to disapprove; in scripture, sometimes to love less.

expand to see more

HATE, v.t. — 1. To dislike greatly; to have a great aversion to. It expresses less than abhor, detest, and abominate, unless pronounced with peculiar emphasis. 2. In scripture, to love less; to regard less than something else. If any man come to me, and hate not his father and mother... (Luke 14:26). The meaning is, to love less than Christ.

HATE, n. — Great dislike or aversion; hatred; detestation.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 97:10 — "Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked."

Romans 12:9 — "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good."

1 John 2:9 — "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now."

Luke 14:26 — "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hate is corrupted in opposite directions by the present age: the therapeutic register treats all hatred as pathology, including the holy hatred of sin and evil Scripture commands—and the activist register weaponizes the word hate against any disagreement with the contemporary moral consensus, so that confessing biblical truth on contested matters is reflexively labeled hate speech.

expand to see more

The therapeutic register cannot recognize holy hatred. Scripture commands the saint to love what God loves and to hate what God hates—ye that love the LORD, hate evil; I hate every false way; abhor that which is evil—and the apostolic and prophetic literature is saturated with the holy hatred of sin, idolatry, and oppression that is the necessary correlate of the love of righteousness. The therapeutic culture has trained the believer to be uncomfortable with the very category. All hate is treated as pathology; all aversion as failure of love; all condemnation of evil as judgmentalism. The result is a Christianity that has lost the moral seriousness of its prophets and apostles, that can sing of love but cannot speak of hating what destroys the souls it loves, and that confuses the soft toleration of evil with the hard love of God for the people evil destroys. Recover the doctrine: love and holy hatred are inseparable; the love that does not hate what kills the beloved is not love but sentiment.

The opposite corruption is the activist register that weaponizes the word hate against any disagreement with the present moral consensus, so that confessing biblical truth on contested matters (abortion, sexual ethics, the exclusivity of Christ) is reflexively labeled hate speech and the speaker treated as a hater rather than as a witness. The biblical distinctions disappear: the holy hatred of sin (commanded) is conflated with personal malice toward sinners (forbidden), and the comparative love of Christ above all (Luke 14:26) is conflated with bigotry against those one is comparatively loving less. Recover the distinctions Scripture itself makes, and the believer regains both his liberty and his courage: he loves the image-bearer warmly even while he hates the sin that destroys him; he loves Christ supremely without ceasing to love family and self in their proper place; he refuses both the therapeutic collapse that calls holy hatred pathological and the activist collapse that calls biblical confession hate.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sānē’ (to hate) and Greek miseō (to hate), used in three distinct biblical registers: the forbidden personal malice toward the brother, the commanded holy hatred of evil, and the comparative idiom of preferring Christ above every other love.

expand to see more

Hebrew sānē’ (H8130) — to hate; used negatively, positively, and comparatively (Gen 29:31, Leah ‘hated’).

Greek miseō (G3404) — to hate (Luke 14:26; 1 John 2:9; Heb 1:9 quoting Ps 45:7).

Greek apostugeō (G655) — to abhor, hate intensely (Rom 12:9).

Greek bdelussomai (G948) — to abominate, detest (Rom 2:22; Rev 21:8).
